summary:
ASTROMIND is a pixel-art game for kids aged 7-12 that turns them into lunar mission engineers. The player lands in a polar crater with a rocket, a 3D printer and eight hours of air. To survive, they print solar panels, charge batteries before the lunar night, drill ice, split water into oxygen, grow food in a greenhouse and hide from solar flares. The goal is a base that keeps the astronaut alive on its own.

For the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge, we turned its four topics (energy, life support, food and radiation) into actions, not text. Every building has a cost: the greenhouse gives food but takes water needed for oxygen. Kids learn to make trade-offs, like real mission engineers.

The simulation uses real data: 0.82 kg of oxygen, 2.5 kg of water and 1.51 kg of food per day (NASA BVAD), 1.369 mSv of radiation per day (Chang'E 4) and a 600 mSv limit (NASA-STD-3001). Many young kids don't read well yet, so a robot helper gives one short hint at a time and arrows show the way. Cadet mode lets the youngest play without losing. The game is open source and runs in a browser.
details:
What it does

ASTROMIND is a 2.5D pixel-art survival and building game for kids aged 7-12. The player is an astronaut who lands in a polar crater on the Moon with a rocket, a 3D printer (fabricator) and eight hours of air in the suit. Step by step they build a base: solar panels and batteries for power, a drill for ice, a water plant, an electrolyzer that splits water into oxygen and hydrogen, an LED greenhouse for food, and a regolith shelter for solar flares. The goal is a base that keeps the astronaut alive on its own.

How it works

Every game hour the astronaut takes 1/24 of the daily oxygen, water and food from base storage. Solar panels give no power at night, so batteries must be built ahead of time. Solar flares come with a two-hour warning, and the radiation dose builds up toward a career limit. A base tablet shows power and supplies at a glance. Every choice has a cost: a second greenhouse gives more food but leaves too little water for oxygen. Kids learn to plan and make trade-offs, the way real mission engineers do.

Real science

The simulation uses real values: 0.82 kg of oxygen, 2.5 kg of water and 1.51 kg of food per astronaut per day (NASA BVAD), 1.369 mSv of radiation per day on the lunar surface (Chang'E 4 LND), a 600 mSv career limit (NASA-STD-3001), -173 to +127 °C surface temperatures (LRO Diviner) and water ice in polar craters (LRO). Learning cards add facts about ISS water recycling, NASA Veggie and Kilopower. Game simplifications, such as a 24-hour lunar day, are listed openly in DATA_SOURCES.md.

Benefits and impact

The game covers all four topics of the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge (power, life support, food and radiation protection) through actions, not text. Many kids in this age group don't read well yet, so a scripted robot helper gives one short hint at a time and arrows and blueprints show where to go. Cadet mode lets the youngest play without losing, and Astronaut mode gives the full challenge. We hope kids finish the game knowing why the Moon is hard to live on and what Artemis astronauts will need to stay alive there.

Tools

Godot 4.7 and GDScript for the game; Blender (with Python scripts) for low-poly 3D models; ElevenLabs Music for the soundtrack; Kenney CC0 assets, Press Start 2P and Cosmic fonts. The game is exported to HTML5 (hosted on Vercel) and to Windows and Linux builds. The code is open source under GPL-3.0. No special hardware is needed: it runs in any modern browser.

Creativity

Instead of a quiz, the child runs a small lunar base, and the science lives inside the mechanics: night drains the batteries, a flare sends you to the shelter. Pixel art, a friendly robot and short sessions make it feel like a game, not a lesson.

What we considered

Age and reading level, so the game can be played almost without text; scientific accuracy, with every number sourced; difficulty, with two modes; and access, so it runs free in a browser on school computers.
